analysis.one_liner: Bars waste from being dumped into waterways disguised as "fill" under the Clean Water Act.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote despite winning 36 cosponsors, including 6 of 223 House Republicans and the chamber's only Independent.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Water Act's definition of "fill material" so that waste could not be dumped into rivers, streams, and wetlands simply by calling it fill. Under the current rule, polluters can get an Army Corps of Engineers permit to bury waters with waste as long as some purpose besides waste disposal is claimed. The bill died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downstream of waters currently receiving waste dumped under Clean Water Act fill permits — their streams would no longer be legally buried by waste. The bill's main practical target was mining waste disposal into valleys and streams, so coalfield communities had the most at stake.

how_it_helps.text: Defines "fill material" under the Federal Water Pollution Control Act as anything that replaces waters of the United States with dry land or changes a water body's bottom elevation, and expressly excludes any pollutant discharged primarily to dispose of waste — closing the permit pathway for dumping waste into waters as "fill" [S2][S3].

Because the Corps of Engineers can authorize fills in waters with a Clean Water Act permit, the definition change would have taken away the legal basis for burying streams and wetlands with waste [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mining companies and other industries that dispose of waste by using it as fill in waterways, since they would have to find and pay for alternative disposal. Coalfield towns whose jobs depend on that cheap disposal method would bear the economic side of the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Waste-discharging mining companies and mining towns

drawbacks.text: The exclusion reaches any pollutant discharged "primarily to dispose of waste," not just mining waste, so it could sweep in other disposal practices that currently rely on fill permits and force costly alternatives [S3].

The bill stops the dumping but leaves the underlying mining or activity itself untouched, so the waste still has to go somewhere — likely onto land near the same communities — and the cheapest disposal option in the coalfields would close, which is a real cost to mining-dependent local economies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is one sentence long but would have a large practical effect: waste could no longer be dumped into the nation's waters under fill permits. The cost falls on the industries that currently dispose of waste that way and on mining towns that rely on the cheap method; the benefit is intact streams and cleaner water for the people who live near and below them. Weighing that trade honestly, the benefit to water quality and public health is broad and lasting, while the cost is real but concentrated and largely a matter of disposal expense shifting back onto the polluter.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its water subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on May 8, 2002, joined at introduction by Rep. Christopher Shays [S3][S5].
The House referred it the same day to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to that committee's Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — the bill never left subcommittee, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that dump waste into waterways under fill permits — above all mining companies — kept the status quo, while the communities living near the affected streams got no new protection.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever happened, so the parties' positions on the floor were never tested; sponsorship was bipartisan, with 29 of 208 Democrats, 6 of 223 Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent signing on, while the Republican-chaired committee buried the bill.

industries.industry: Coal mining (mountaintop removal and valley fills)
industries.note: The bill's exclusion of waste from the fill-material definition would take away the Clean Water Act permit pathway that mountaintop removal operations use to bury streams and valleys with mine waste. Coalfield communities gain cleaner water; the industry gains nothing and loses its cheapest disposal method.

industries.industry: Industries disposing of waste as fill (dredging, construction, hard-rock mining)
industries.note: Any pollutant discharged primarily to dispose of waste would be barred from use as fill, so other industries that get rid of waste by filling in waters would have to pay for alternative disposal.
